title: Soloing on chords in 1918 versus the 1927 Charlie Johnson records
summary: Waters insists he soloed on chord changes in 1918 as now. He says he plays better today, was better on alto than the tenor Charlie Johnson made him switch to, and copied Hawkins's slap tongue on the 1927 records.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

Well, I could, I could have been playin' better first thing if I was playin' alto, that's the first thing. And that was my first instrument, and I was better on alto than I was on tenor. That's the first thing. And I could have been playing better construction of harmonies and things on the alto at that period. Then in the meantime, when I made those records with Charlie Johnson at that, at down in Camden at Victor, my inspiration was Coleman Hawkins, it was that slap tongue. You can even hear it on the record, I made a break whence [?], took the slap tongue in each note. And that was taken strictly from Coleman Hawkins. See, so I was copying then. But during that period you're talkin' about, it was not the copy, I'm just playing from my natural ability, that's what I'm trying to bring out for you, to you. I'm just playing from my natural ability, and it couldn't have been better, good thing that I'm on the horn that I loved, the first thing. Like I told you then, when I came here, when I changed to tenor, it was wished on me. It wasn't my idea, it was Charlie Johnson said "He can't play choruses, and would you" - asked me as a favor - "would you change with him and give him your alto and you play tenor?" You see what I mean? See, so I could have been playing much

better because I was changed to a horn that I wasn't even familiar with, see what I mean? Very well, very easily be playing more. I don't know, people have all kinds of things 'cause I've advanced a lot by listening. But I still think I play alto better. I think I'm more handy with the alto, I still think so. Well, that's proof that I know what I'm talking from beginning back there, I'm now, today - I think I'm more handy with the alto. I do more tricks, I can get over the horn, I can even play more modern, if you listen real carefully on the alto, you know? So that's proof of what we talking about, see. So I could have been playing better then, just from natural ability and not listening, see.
